intros.text: Micah lived during the eighth century b.c. The speeches collected in this book were warnings of the Lord's judgment against two cities: Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and Jerusalem, the capital of the southern kingdom of Judah. Micah courageously speaks out against injustice. He accuses the rich of oppressing the poor and condemns the worship of pagan idols, the cruelty of rulers, and the lies told by priests and prophets who care more for money than for God. He prophesies that Jerusalem will be left in ruins and the temple will become a barren mountain. But Micah also announces a future time of peace and prosperity, when the Lord will lead his people home and bring to power a new ruler who will bring peace and who will be known and honored throughout the world. In the book's concluding poems, Micah says that God's people will praise the Lord for keeping the agreement he made with their ancestor Abraham. Outline Messages of Judgment against Israel and Judah (1.1—3.12) Messages of Hope for God's People (4.1—5.15) The LORD Puts the People of Israel on Trial for Their Sins (6.1—7.7) The LORD Forgives Those Who Confess Their Sins (7.8-20)

verses.text: I am Micah from Moresheth. And this is the message about Samaria and Jerusalem that the LORD gave to me when Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah were the kings of Judah.

footnotes.text: Moresheth: A town in southern Judah not far from Gath. In verse 14 it is called Moresheth-Gath.
Samaria and Jerusalem: Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom (Israel), and Jerusalem was the capital of the southern kingdom (Judah).
Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah: Jotham, the son of Uzziah, ruled Judah 740–736 b.c.; Ahaz, the son of Jotham, ruled 736–716 b.c.; Hezekiah, the son of Ahaz, ruled 716–687 b.c.

verses.text: Listen, all of you! Earth and everything on it, pay close attention. The LORD God accuses you from his holy temple.

footnotes.text: holy temple: Possibly the one in heaven, though it may be the Jerusalem temple.

verses.text: And he will come down to crush underfoot every pagan altar.
Mountains will melt beneath his feet like wax beside a fire. Valleys will vanish like water rushing down a ravine.
This will happen because of the terrible sins of Israel, the descendants of Jacob. Samaria has led Israel to sin, and pagan altars at Jerusalem have made Judah sin.
So the LORD will leave Samaria in ruins— merely an empty field where vineyards are planted. He will scatter its stones and destroy its foundations.
Samaria's idols will be smashed, and the wages of temple prostitutes will be destroyed by fire. Silver and gold from those idols will then be used by foreigners as payment for prostitutes.

footnotes.text: wages of temple prostitutes: At pagan temples, people had sex with prostitutes as a way of worshiping the idols, and the money earned in this way was used to support the pagan religion.

verses.text: Because of this tragedy, I go barefoot and naked. My crying and weeping sound like howling wolves or ostriches.

footnotes.text: this tragedy: Either the destruction of Samaria (verses 6,7) or the coming destruction of Judah and Jerusalem.

verses.text: The nation is fatally wounded. Judah is doomed. Jerusalem will fall.
Don't tell it in Gath! Don't even cry. Instead, roll in the dust at Beth-Leaphrah.

footnotes.text: Gath … Beth-Leaphrah: Gath was a Philistine city; Beth-Leaphrah is unknown, but in Hebrew it sounds like “House of Dust.”

verses.text: Depart naked and ashamed, you people of Shaphir. The town of Bethezel mourns because no one from Zaanan went out to help.

footnotes.text: Shaphir: Mentioned only here in the Old Testament; in Hebrew “Shaphir” means “beautiful.”
Bethezel: Mentioned only here in the Old Testament; in Hebrew “Bethezel” means “house next door.”
Zaanan: Mentioned only here in the Old Testament; in Hebrew “Zaanan” means “one who goes out.”
The town … help: Or “No one from Zaanan refused to desert their town, and Bethezel mourns because it is left undefended.”

verses.text: Everyone in Maroth hoped for the best, but the LORD sent disaster down on Jerusalem.

footnotes.text: Maroth: Mentioned only here in the Old Testament; in Hebrew “Maroth” means “bitter.”

verses.text: Get the war chariots ready, you people of Lachish. You led Jerusalem into sin, just as Israel did.

footnotes.text: Lachish: The chief city of southwest Judah, about 48 kilometers from Jerusalem.

led … sin … did: Or “You led Jerusalem and Israel into sin.” In Hebrew “Lachish” sounds like “a team of horses (that pulls a war chariot).” And the sin may be that Lachish led the nation to trust the power of war chariots instead of the LORD. But the sin could be idolatry or some false teachings that were brought in from Egypt by way of Lachish.

verses.text: Now you will have to give a going-away gift to Moresheth. Israel's kings will discover that they cannot trust the town of Achzib.

footnotes.text: going-away gift: The gift (dowry) that a bride's father gave her when she left the home of her parents to live with the family of her husband. In Hebrew the word for “bride” or “fiancee” sounds like “Moresheth.”
Moresheth: Hebrew “Moresheth-Gath”; the home of Micah (see verse 1).

Achzib: Meaning “lie” or “deception” was near Adullam Cave (verse 15), where David hid from King Saul (see 1 Samuel 22.1,2). Micah probably means that the people of Israel (including their king) will have to run for their lives, but will find that all hope for escape is merely a “lie” (see verse 15).

verses.text: People of Mareshah, the LORD will send someone to capture your town. Then Israel's glorious king will be forced to hide in Adullam Cave.

footnotes.text: Mareshah: Sounds something like the Hebrew word for “conqueror” and was only a few kilometers northeast of Lachish.
Adullam Cave: See the note at 1.14.

verses.text: Judah, shave your head as bald as a vulture and start mourning. Your precious children will be dragged off to a foreign country.

footnotes.text: precious children: The towns mentioned in verses 10-15.
